Botvice presents itself as a simple 2D bullet hell shooter and then quietly rewires the part of your brain that craves this specific kind of punishment until you've consumed somewhere north of a dozen hours without fully understanding how you got there.

What it's doing mechanically is not revolutionary. The genre has established rules and Botvice largely respects them, projectiles fill the screen, you find the safe space, you survive by fractions of a second, you die anyway, you try again. The loop is old. The execution is clean enough that the loop doesn't care that it's old.

The interesting clinical observation is what happens after. Bullet hell games operate on a very specific neurological reward cycle and Botvice delivers that cycle efficiently enough that by the time you've finished it the appetite has been largely satisfied. Not extinguished, satisfied. The itch has been properly scratched in a way that leaves you not necessarily hungry for the next one immediately, which is either a sign of a complete experience or a sign that the genre extracts something from you that requires recovery time. Possibly both.

Worth diagnosing for yourself at sale price. The Steam Deck is the ideal environment for this particular experiment, short sessions, immediate feedback, no commitment required. Pick it up, put it down, come back when the symptoms return.

Recommended with the caveat that you may emerge from the other side temporarily cured of wanting anything like it. Whether that's a positive outcome depends entirely on your relationship with the genre going in.

Bot Vice is a compact but fiercely intense arcade-style shooter developed and published by DYA Games that embraces old-school design philosophies while injecting them with modern polish and relentless pacing. From the moment the game begins, it makes its priorities clear: precision, reflexes, and mastery of movement matter far more than elaborate systems or extended exposition. Bot Vice is unapologetically focused on delivering short, high-adrenaline bursts of action that reward practice and punish complacency, echoing the spirit of classic arcade cabinets where every second counted and every mistake was costly.

The premise is straightforward and deliberately pulpy. Players step into the role of Erin Saver, a former cop turned cybernetic vigilante waging a one-woman war against a criminal robot syndicate known as the Wildbots. Having already lost both her partner and part of her own body to these mechanical enemies, Erin’s crusade is driven by vengeance and survival rather than heroism. The story exists largely to frame the action, delivered through brief text and visual cues, and it never distracts from the core experience. This minimalist narrative approach works in the game’s favor, keeping momentum high and attention firmly locked on the battlefield.

Gameplay is built around single-screen stages packed with enemies, hazards, and projectile patterns that demand constant movement and awareness. Erin can dash, slide, shoot, and take limited cover, but survival depends on understanding enemy behaviors and anticipating attack patterns rather than relying on raw firepower. One of Bot Vice’s defining design choices is its automatic targeting system, which removes the need for manual aiming and allows players to concentrate fully on positioning, dodging, and timing. This creates a smooth, almost rhythmic flow to combat, where success feels earned through spatial awareness and pattern recognition rather than twitch aiming.

Despite the brevity of individual stages, the game’s challenge curve is steep and deliberate. Early levels introduce core mechanics at a manageable pace, but difficulty ramps up quickly as enemy formations grow denser and bullet patterns more aggressive. Boss fights serve as major skill checks, each one introducing unique mechanics that force players to adapt rather than rely on memorized strategies. These encounters are tense and often punishing, but rarely feel unfair, as failures are almost always traceable to player error rather than arbitrary design.

Replayability is central to Bot Vice’s appeal. Levels are short enough to encourage repeated attempts, and improvement comes naturally as players learn enemy timings, safe zones, and optimal movement paths. Additional modes and challenges extend the game’s lifespan, offering tougher scenarios that push even experienced players to refine their skills further. There are no sprawling progression trees or RPG-style upgrades; improvement is tied directly to player mastery, reinforcing the arcade ethos at the heart of the experience.

Visually, the game adopts a vibrant pixel-art style that balances clarity with personality. Enemies, bullets, and environmental hazards are easy to distinguish even when the screen fills with chaos, which is crucial in a game where split-second decisions can mean the difference between survival and failure. Character animations are fluid, and explosions and effects add satisfying feedback without obscuring vital information. The aesthetic leans heavily into retro influences while maintaining a clean, readable presentation suited to fast-paced play.

Audio design complements the visuals with high-energy music and punchy sound effects that reinforce the game’s intensity. The soundtrack draws inspiration from synth-heavy arcade and action music, keeping adrenaline levels high throughout repeated runs. Sound cues provide important feedback during combat, signaling enemy attacks or successful hits, and help players stay oriented during particularly hectic moments.

Community reception has consistently highlighted Bot Vice’s tight controls, demanding but fair difficulty, and strong arcade identity. Players who enjoy classic shooters and bullet-hell-inspired design often praise the game for respecting their time while still offering meaningful challenge. Criticism tends to focus on its limited scope and lack of deeper systems, but these aspects are intrinsic to its design philosophy rather than oversights. Bot Vice is not trying to be expansive; it is focused, deliberate, and sharply defined.

Taken as a whole, Bot Vice is a confident and disciplined arcade shooter that succeeds by knowing exactly what it wants to be. It delivers fast, skill-driven action in concentrated doses, blending retro sensibilities with modern responsiveness and visual clarity. For players who crave intense, replayable challenges and appreciate games that reward practice and precision over progression mechanics, Bot Vice stands as a strong example of how much impact a tightly designed indie shooter can deliver in a small package.

This game is insanely good once you start getting used to the controls.  I just wanted to check it out for a min, ended playing though the whole campaign in one sitting, plus played 6 of the bonus missions which ended up being over two hours.  Be warned, this game doesn't mess around and immediately throws you into the action.  One of the early levels already has a skill check (I think it was 1-4) and it had me retry it at least 20 times before getting passed.  Luckily, each level is super short and dying give you an instant restart (which I LOVE when games do that).  Each and every weapon feels amazing to use and certain ones are great to have in certain situations, so there is a lot of strategy you need to use on the fly. 

The bosses don't seem to be as hard as the levels, with the exception of the last one, but they are still really fun to learn.  There is a huge amount of enemy variety and when they are all on the screen at once, it is complete chaos, but in a good way.  There are 3 ways to dodge, one by slashing the bullets with your short range sword, one by using cover that can be broken by the enemy, and the other is by using the dodge roll button that has no cooldown, but can often bring you out of the dodge on top of of bullet.  All three are useful in different situations and eventually have to be mastered to make progress.  Gameplay wise, this is about as good as it gets. 

The pixel art is always pretty to look at, the music is a steady synthwave bop, and the voice acting is... not that great, but I like that it is there anyways.  The main character's voice is kinda dull and the enemies all seem to be played by the same voice actor, who does a pretty decent job overall with only one exception.  The achievements are actually something fun to get by adding extra challenges to the stages, and there is a scoring system, so there is a decent amount of replayability.  And as I mentioned, there are bonus stages that almost double to content of the game.  

This was seriously some of the most fun I have had in quite a while and I highly recommend it for people who enjoy arcade-style action games that take a lot of skill to master.  Even at full price, it is a good deal.

In terms of presentation, it's great. In terms of gameplay, it's not.

There's way too much going on at once. Too many enemies, too many projectiles, too many other objects on screen. It might not be so bad if you had more control over your character, but you're limited to side-to-side movement and an aim lock. Manual aim with a mouse would make this so much more tolerable, since the auto aim has a habit of locking onto enemies you don't want it to or firing your weapons at an angle where you can't hit the target at all.

I may have been doing something wrong, because there were a few mechanics I didn't even use. You have a sword which the game tells you is "very powerful and can destroy enemy projectiles" but enemies will rarely get close enough for you to use it on them and it's easier to just dodge their projectiles than destroy them. It's a similar story for the crouch that lets you hide behind cover, I never used it because dodging is made out to be better and easier.

Finally, enemies have a bad habit of sticking to the very back of the battlefield behind indestructible objects, meaning they can continue to attack you whilst you can do nothing to fight back. They also frequently stand near objects you aren't meant to shoot (one of the early levels has 2 objects that spawn additional enemies if you shoot them, and those enemies can't be locked onto) but it's impossible to deal with them effectively due to the shoddy auto aim.
Intense and catchy, but difficult AF.

Bot Vice is a challenging game, which on occasion left me (positively) frustrated. This game offers fast paced gameplay, with a screen full of different enemies types and mechanics to deal with. Your variety of weaponry is ripped straight from the Time Crisis series and each have their uses and were a lot of fun to use. 25 Levels in story mode, another 25 in Extra Missions, each of which can be completed in as little as a minute, if you are effecient enough. 

Gameplay really comes down to target priority and reaction time. Enemies dont really telegraph before attacking and when faced with multiple, its easy to get overwhelmed. Success is continuously strafing and rolling. The cover mechanic is important, but over-reliance will see your cover destroyed and eventually leaving you exposed and a sitting duck. ALWAYS. BE. ROLLING.

 Sound and visuals remind me of classic Capcom/Namco titles. Voice acting came off as light hearted, silly, and wasnt taken seriously. Bot Vice is a lot of fun. If you are looking a challenging arcade shooter, give this one a go.

Well Bot Vice is a pretty good time. It's got a really good foundation that is held back by some odd controls and rather tough gameplay. 
Bot Vice puts you at the bottom area of the screen, moving left and right through running, dashing rolling, or crouching. You're goal is to clear the enemies flooding the top of the screen. Each enemy has a different attack pattern you need to learn so as to dodge their incoming damage. This is where the first difficulty rise shows it's head. Some of these patterns can create just chaos on the screen. While you can crouch at any time to put the damage on your blockade, it becomes impossible to find moments to pop up and shoot. So taking damage is your only way (Keep this in mind).
You are given different types of weapons to clear your enemies out faster. You are required to cycle through them in a left to right fashion. I think a weapon wheel to get directly to the weapon you desire would help, but the voice shouting your selection is helpful. Some of your weapons include things like Spreadshots, rapid fire, actual fire, or rockets/grenades. Some weapons are nearly required to kill some enemies.
Now this part is only important if you are going for 100%. There are some tough ones. Most levels have an achievement attached that require some side objective to be completed. These can range from simply don't get hit by a certain attack, all the way to do not hit a certain destructible items in the level. Which can be difficult in the chaos considering...
The lock on. It is not precise at all. You will be locked on and even if the enemy is standing still as are you, you will not be actually shooting at the enemy. This can cause a lot of frustration at times when you need at angle. Other times when you roll the lock on deactivates only to lock onto someone else, which can throw off what you are doing. It turns into a bit of a mess at times.
Other achievements include getting an A or above on all levels, which is usually just how fast you beat it. This usually isn't that bad if you use your other weapons.   
The last big achievement is getting 4 hearts each level. This means ending the level with 4 hearts. You'll see during play that there is a bot that will drop hearts, so at the start you'll think you can just take a few hits and collect hearts back to full. But that isn't an option. That bot only drops *A* heart when you've lost 2 hearts. Meaning to get 4 hearts on every level, each level must be beaten without being hit. Remember earlier about some moments requiring a hit to finally get a shot in. Yeah... That was a killer achievement. It was rough and a pain to finish. 
Over all, this game is a blast to play. But man it's got a few quirks to it that take it to that frustrating level at times. I recommend this game at full price though. Just maybe spread out your play session and keep them in short bursts. That will make your time with it fully enjoyable.

Bot Vice é um Shoot em Up 2D estilo Arcade com visão Top-Down e elementos de Bullet Hell, o jogo conta com uma mecânica de gameplay única e muito tiro na tela, se garante principalmente com seus gráficos pixel art e jogabilidade frenética com dificuldade bastante elevada ao estilo jogos de fliperama. 

[h1]História[/h1] 
Passa-se em Bot City, você joga como Erin Saver, uma ex-policial que virou vigilante. Seis meses antes dos acontecimentos do jogo, Erin perseguia uma gangue criminosa conhecida como Wildbots, liderada por quatro ciborgues mercenários porém ela perdeu o seu parceiro além de seu braço direito, e desde então deixou a polícia. Agora, seis meses depois, os Wildbots foram contratados por um homem conhecido simplesmente como “Lunático” que assumiu o controle do edifício Tominaka Plaza e ameaça destruí-lo a menos que receba cem bilhões de botcoins. Agora equipada com um braço biônico, Erin faz justiça com as próprias mãos e decide deter o Lunático e os Wildbots. O jogo conta com uma mini introdução explicando a história e algumas cutscenes ao longo do jogo que ainda assim não é tão aprofundada, são backgrounds com caixas de texto e algumas poucas animações, é óbvio que a história não era realmente o ponto principal, mas tá lá para quem quiser entender todo contexto. 

[h1]Gráficos[/h1] 
Bot Vice é um jogo bastante bonito visualmente ainda mais se você for fã de jogos Arcade clássicos como os de Neo Geo ou algo próximo dos jogos de Gameboy Advance por exemplo. É feito em pixel art, colorido e bem detalhado que agrada aos olhos. As explosões e efeitos dos diversos tipos de tiros são bem feitas e tornam a killcount de robôs muito mais satisfatória e viciante, a parte da chuva de balas também é ótima, trocentos disparos coloridos de todo canto na sua direção e as vezes você fica perdido em meio a tanta coisa na tela (o que é bom já que é uma particularidade do gênero) os inimigos embora bem simples devido ao estilo artístico, são bem feitos assim como a protagonista Erin todos tem ótimas animações, os cenários são mais simples com camadas de objetos que variam conforme progresso das fases, mas são bonitos também e tem uma boa variedade de lugares.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Ja na sua gameplay, Bot Vice é um jogo de tiro em galeria então Erin só pode se mover para a esquerda e para a direita até o limite da fase. Ela pode atirar para frente ou focar nos inimigos com mira automática e rolar para evitar ataques (você é invencível enquanto rola e pode fazer com frequência pra evitar dano) além disso também é possível pegar cobertura atrás de objetos (muitas vezes me pegava entrando ou saindo da cobertura quando não era minha intenção) uma pena que não haja a opção de alternar durante um cover por exemplo, então pra facilitar deixei setado como analógico pra baixo. Você não pode atirar enquanto estiver protegido, então precisará se expor. Cada estágio tem uma linha de objetos à sua frente que constituem a cobertura e a cobertura pode ser destruída pelos inimigos, então não é aconselhável permanecer no mesmo local. Não só isso, mas os inimigos lançarão bombas e tiros que podem acerta-lo mesmo se você estiver protegido, portanto, saber quando rolar, entrar na cobertura e atacar é crucial para o sucesso nesse jogo. Erin só pode ser atingida quatro vezes antes de morrer e se você morrer precisará reiniciar a fase. 

Pequenos robôs amarelos voarão pelos ambientes e atirar neles fará com que eles percam saúde e dropem um item coletável de arma, o Arsenal é composto por metralhadora que dispara rapidamente embora tenha um dano mais baixo, já a Spread Gun é ótima para destruir vários inimigos ao mesmo tempo ja que os tiros espalham. Temos um lança-chamas, ótima para curto alcance ou quando inimigos estiver perto do cover e o lançador de foguetes e lança-granadas, são as armas mais mortíferas do jogo, ótimas para desintegrar rapidamente alguns dos inimigos mais difíceis/com mais vida. Alem disso Erin conta com um poderoso Sabre podendo usar para destruir inimigos que se aproximem demais e até mesmo destruir projéteis que se aproximam. Erin está sempre equipada com uma arma com munição infinita, mas as outras armas são muito melhores, embora todas com munição limitada. 

Seu objetivo no jogo é bastante simples: você terá um determinado tempo para completar todas as 25 fases do jogo, o tempo é subtraído com base em quanto você leva para completar cada fase, então você vai querer vencê-las o mais rápido possível. Você pode repetir qualquer fase já concluída e cada uma delas pode ser vencida em menos de dois minutos (felizmente, consegui zerar 8 minutos antes do tempo acabar) cada fase tem um boss e a cada cinco fases você terá que lutar contra um dos ciborgues casca grossa dos Wildbots. Depois de vencer a campanha, você desbloqueará mais 25 missões extras, com mais uma boa dose de conteúdo endgame. Mesmo que as fases sejam curtas, algumas delas podem ser extremamente difíceis e você precisará usar tudo que tiver em seu arsenal para sobreviver, e quando eu digo difícil é difícil mesmo! Existem três modos de dificuldade: Fácil, Normal e Difícil, joguei principalmente no Normal e mesmo no Normal o jogo pode ser bastante punitivo, não consigo imaginar o quão desafiador deve ser no Hard.

Bot Vice é aquele tipo de jogo de tiro intenso que vai te frustrar até você melhorar, a abertura do tutorial mostra tudo o que você precisa saber e cabe a você dominar os controles para ter sucesso. Não há curva de aprendizado, nem subida de nível, nem power-ups e nada que realmente ajude você, praticamente ou você fica bom ou morre. O jogo fica mais difícil conforme você avança e as missões extras irão realmente te desafiar. Os inimigos podem voar, teletransportar-se, alguns têm escudos e outros dos inimigos mais irritantes como os robôs sapos, pularão sobre você. Os chefes incluem coisas como tanques, aeronaves, diferentes tipos de veículos, inimigos robóticos mais difíceis e coisas nesse sentido. Depois de vencer uma fase, você recebe uma classificação de letra que acredito ser baseada no tempo e na quantidade de saúde que lhe restou. O valor replay vem na forma de tentar completar cada fase mais rápido possível e alcançar as classificações mais altas. Eu sou péssimo em jogo assim, por isso era muito raro conseguir classificações altas, mas é tudo uma questão de prática e memorização. 

Os efeitos sonoros são decentes, alguns dos inimigos tem vozes robóticas estereotipadas, os sons de tiros e explosões são bons, mas é a música/OST que realmente é a melhor parte sonora desse jogo. Bot Vice está cheio de synth-rock dos anos 90 com um toque de estilo 16 bits algo próximo de Chiptunes de SNES por exemplo. De qualquer forma, a OST é incrível, cada música é cativante e eletrizante, se você curte esse estilo de música e/ou algo próximo de músicas de jogos de GBA, deveria ouvir seriamente a trilha sonora.  Completo com um modo de história, missões extras e suporte total ao controle, Bot Vice é um Shoot em Up cheio de ação onde você atira em todos os tipos de inimigos robóticos com objetivo de derrotar um louco, a história realmente não se leva a sério, mas felizmente a jogabilidade e OST é viciante pra compensar isso.

Bot Vice é um dos jogos indies mais divertidos que joguei, ótimo pra passar o tempo, embora extremamente difícil e depende muito do seu reflexo estar em dia, é uma pérola muito boa e divertida assim como boa parte dos jogos da DYA Games, um jogo intenso e rápido que se você curtir, irá mantê-lo envolvido do começo ao fim. É extremamente desafiador e graças ao sistema de classificação e aos modos de dificuldade, há uma boa taxa de re-jogabilidade, tem alguns pequenos problemas, mas a jogabilidade é tão viciante que eles passam facilmente despercebidos: você pode jogar como uma garota com braço biônico e explodir robôs com um arsenal satisfatório, preciso dizer mais alguma coisa? Comprei por 6 conto na Steam, e definitivamente recomendaria o Bot Vice para aficionados no gênero.
